title: Negative pressure wound therapy
intro: Negative pressure wound therapy seals a special dressing over a wound and connects it to a pump that gently removes fluid by suction. It is used for wounds that heal slowly, such as pressure sores, diabetic foot ulcers and some surgical wounds. It may speed healing in some cases, but evidence on its benefit varies.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: A piece of foam or gauze is placed in the wound and covered with an airtight film. A tube links it to a portable pump that applies continuous or intermittent low suction. The aim is to draw out excess fluid, reduce swelling, bring wound edges together and stimulate new tissue.

sections.heading: When it is used
paragraphs: Doctors consider it for large, deep or slow-healing wounds, wounds left open after surgery, burns, skin grafts and infected wounds after cleaning. It is applied after dead tissue has been removed. It is not suitable for wounds with untreated bone infection, cancer in the wound, exposed blood vessels or organs, or some bleeding risks.

sections.heading: What to expect
paragraphs: The dressing is changed every few days by trained staff, and some patients use portable devices at home with nurse visits. You may feel pulling or pain, especially at dressing changes, and pain relief can be given. Report increased pain, bleeding, fever, a foul smell or alarms from the device.

sections.heading: Benefits and uncertainties
paragraphs: Studies suggest the therapy can reduce healing time in some wounds, such as diabetic foot wounds, but for many others the evidence is limited or mixed. Risks include bleeding, pain and skin irritation. Continue other measures such as pressure relief, blood sugar control, good nutrition and stopping smoking, which are essential for healing.

sections.heading: Everyday practicalities
paragraphs: Carry the pump in its bag, protect the dressing when washing and keep the seal intact. Ask about activity limits and how to handle alarms, and keep contact details for the wound team to hand.

examples.title: Managing at home
examples.text: Imagine you go home with a portable pump after surgery. You could ask the nurse how to recognise a leak, whom to call at night and when the next dressing change is.

examples.title: Weighing the options
examples.text: Suppose your foot ulcer has not improved in weeks. You might ask whether negative pressure therapy is suitable, what evidence supports it for your wound and what alternatives exist.
